title: File System Interface
body:
The half-dozen [[System Call|system calls]] a program uses to get at a [[File]], and the
model of a file they imply. [[File Systems]] owns how any of it is implemented on disk;
this note is the view from user space.

| Call | Does |
|---|---|
| `open` | look the name up, check permissions, return a **file descriptor** |
| `read` / `write` | move bytes at the current offset, and advance it |
| `seek` | move the offset without transferring anything |
| `close` | release the descriptor and flush buffers |

## The file descriptor is the point

`open` does the expensive work once (walk the [[Directory]] path, find the inode, check
permissions) and hands back a small integer. Every later call names that integer instead of
the path, so the kernel does not re-resolve the name on every read. The descriptor indexes
a per-process table in the [[PCB]]; the entry it points at holds the current offset and the
access mode.

Consequences worth noticing:

- The offset lives in the *open file*, not in the file and not in the process. Two
  independent `open` calls on one file get independent offsets.
- Descriptors are inherited across `fork`, which is precisely how [[Piping]] connects two
  processes: the shell hands one end to each child.

## A file is a stream of bytes, and nothing else

Unix deliberately gives the file no structure: no records, no fields, no types. Meaning is
the application's problem. That is why **the same four calls work on a
[[File]], a [[FIFO|named pipe]], a terminal, and a socket**, and why
`ls -l | grep md` can work at all: `grep` cannot tell a pipe from a file, so it does not
have to care.

A `read` that cannot be satisfied yet (empty pipe, disk not ready) blocks the process into
the [[Waiting state]] rather than returning garbage. That is the same blocking-versus-not
argument [[Node.js]] makes one layer up.
